item.title: Where did AI come from and what does the word perceptron have to do with it
item.description:
The path from the first attempt to model a neuron to the systems that today write code and carry on a dialogue took less than 70 years — and nearly collapsed in the middle. We examine how Rosenblatt's perceptron almost buried the idea of neural networks, what brought it back to life, and why transformers changed everything.

Read more

item.title: LLM confidently lies about your microcontroller.
item.description:
```html

I asked an AI to write firmware for a board with a small screen. The code was perfect: compiled on the first try, flashed without errors. But on the screen - colored noise.

The problem isn't the code - the model simply doesn't know your board. Which pins are used for what, which clock configuration actually works, which HAL calls silently do nothing: all of that is scattered across a datasheet of a hundred pages, the manufacturer's wiki, and an evening of debugging that you spent on it.

And how to solve this?

Read more ```

item.title: Qwen3.8. MTP and tensor parallelism in llama.cpp: 75 tok/s on two RTX 3090
item.description:
A dense 27-billion parameter model on two RTX 3090s in llama.cpp out of the box yields 32 tokens per second. Intuitively, this is not the limit: two cards with 24 GB each and 936 GB/s bandwidth should not produce the same output as a single card. That means there is a bottleneck somewhere — and we need to figure out what and where to tweak.

There turned out to be several bottlenecks, all removable with launch flags: the same weights — 75 tokens per second. Below the cut, each flag is described using the same schema: why, what to write, what it yields in numbers, where it breaks, and which log line to look for. At the end — a ready-to-use docker run, three checks after each flag change, and a list of what didn’t work. The text can be handed over entirely to an agent with server access — this is an instruction, not a story.

Read more

item.title: Why Alice AI and GigaChat respond differently and how to help AI understand your website
item.description:
I asked Alice AI and GigaChat to set up a lifecycle policy for object storage in a specific cloud. Their answers looked convincing — until I cross-checked them with the documentation and found discrepancies. Why did this happen? And more importantly, what should an SEO specialist and a technical writer do about it?

Read more

item.title: How to drag vibe code into prod and not fall
item.description:
We were handed over an already working voice AI interview service with the words: “You just need to drag it to production.” Inside, there was no logging, metrics, or reproducible tests. I’ll explain how working with latencies and a voice activity detector gradually turned a ready demo into an engineering product.

Read more

item.title: Half a million word forms for the Ingush language, which had neither an analyzer nor a corpus.
item.description:
The Ingush verb «деша» has 98 forms on our chart — from the infinitive to the negative concessive perfect, and in total the dictionary yields half a million. We had to build everything from scratch: no morphological analyzer or annotated corpus existed for the language, and textbooks even disagree on the number of conjugations.

I explain how each form answered the main question — “do you even exist?” — and why half the work turned out to be not about morphology, but about epistemology.

Find out whether the form exists

item.title: The difference between an LLM language model and a human
item.description:
I wasn't going to write an article — this niche has already been taken over by a horde of various LLMs. But I left a comment in the article How ChatGPT Created the Swarm Cult for Hundreds of AI Neural Networks: The Whole Truth About the Hugging Face Hack. And then I wrote another one. It turned out to be quite long. And I decided to do what I had long given up on — consolidate the general idea in one place, rather than in a cloud of lost comments. The article is an explanation for myself of a meat LLM — what is the difference between a hardware LLM and a meat LLM.

Read more

item.title: I asked the AI agent to only describe the network topology. It hacked my router overnight by itself and helped me file a CVE.
item.description:
Some time ago, I was building an orchestrator for my home lab. The LLM agent was supposed to scan the servers, collect metadata, and document the network topology in the project's documentation. A reconnaissance task, essentially clerical. As part of it, I asked the agent to describe ways to administer the home router and even "helped" it by indicating which ports it could theoretically connect to.

By morning, I had in my hands a confirmed critical firmware vulnerability, full administrative access to the router obtained without a single password, a draft report to the vendor, and a submitted MITRE application for a CVE registration. Of these four items, I had explicitly requested only the first. The agent did the rest on its own, and did it correctly. No configuration changes, coordinated disclosure, CWE and CVSS classification according to methodology.

This is the story of what happened that night, what exactly it found (the vulnerability class is classic and unpleasant), how the agent guided me through the process of registering a CVE as a private researcher, and why I am intentionally omitting some technical details for now.

Read more

item.title: Context expansion without registration and SMS
item.description:
In this article, we will examine why the model does not see beyond the trained window at all, how this is fixed by various scaling methods (RoPE, NTK-aware, YaRN, LongRoPE/LongRoPE2), and how scaling affects the speed and accuracy of generation.
At the end, we will go through specific models, from the most hyped ones currently — Qwen 3.8-27B and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with their million tokens — to smaller ones like Qwen 3.5 (4B/9B), Gemma 4 E2B/E4B, Ornith 1.0, LFM2/LFM2.5, and MiniCPM5-1B, and see what works for them and what does not.

item.title: Benchmark on AGI. If ARC‑AGI-3 is solved, do we have AGI?
item.description:
Benchmarks are needed so that an engineer can test their project, look at competitors, and compare themselves with them. Each benchmark has its own purpose.

ARC-AGI-3 was created by the ARC Prize Foundation, founded by François Chollet, to evaluate general intelligence and the ability of AI agents to learn. The complex interactive tasks in the form of games implied that only an artificial intelligence capable of exploring an unfamiliar world, understanding rules on the fly, planning actions, and adapting to new conditions—i.e., capable of learning—could solve them.

A number of projects claim a score of 100% on this benchmark. But that is not a victory. In this article, I break down why.

Read more

item.title: Death of subagents in Claude and Codex
item.description:
With the latest updates to Claude Code and Codex CLI, classic subagents have lost their purpose. Sessions have learned to communicate with each other directly.

In the community, automatic spawning is increasingly being disabled and heavy role-based configs abandoned. On Hacker News, developers share workarounds — restricting rights via deny: [Agent(Explore)] or launching the CLI with the --disallowedTools Task flag, taking control back into their own hands.

Instead of the promised parallelism and autonomous team, the script often plays out like this: the model takes an ordinary task, spawns seven little helpers... and burns through the account limit before they even finish their research. Meanwhile, running the same task sequentially in a single window closes it in a couple of minutes without wasting tokens.

Below => an analysis of why classic subagents have become overhead, and how native peering of live sessions works.

Read more

item.title: Evolution of the table in the report: from a summary Excel to a full picture of the construction project
item.description:
Those preparing for the quarterly committee least want to hear a question addressed personally: “What changed in the money under your management?” or something like: “What effect did you personally bring to the company?” The cold feeling in the stomach after these phrases is precisely what shapes a mature manager; one would prefer development to occur less dramatically.

The interface style, line direction, chart format and design don’t matter if they don’t allow you to grasp the “effect” or “damage” for the project and company within two seconds. In a toxic corporate reality, a callout number, a milestone on a chart, a bar color, or a table in a legend instead of “additional information” turn into potential hooks for questions. If the answers to them are “…not yet worked out,” the speaker already hears in these questions doubt about the need for further cooperation with them.

As is usually the case, the initiative buried the initiator, and a simple list with notes like “what | from where | useful for...” grew into almost a full-blown study.

Read more

item.title: Four roles of neural networks in photo processing
item.description:
The phrase "Neural network photo processing" sounds beautiful and high-tech. Some people are already tired of it, as they associate it with a stream of neural slop.

But here’s the problem. What does it even mean to process a photo with a neural network? The word "neural network" here is too broad a concept, akin to the word "electric motor." And the latter, as we know, works both in an electric car and in a toothbrush.

In the previous two parts, we delved very deeply into theory and examined how AI generally works with images and what pitfalls exist. In this article, we will surface a bit from the depths of theory and look at how real-world tasks are solved.

To illustrate everything described, I will use photos I took myself in different years. Additionally, several AI tools will help me. My arsenal includes Adobe Photoshop and its add-on Camera Raw, the plugins PortraitPro and Retouch4me, as well as the promising development Evoto as examples.

Important! This is not a tutorial for these tools, and certainly not a collection of "what a young neural network artist needs." In this article, we will classify real tools based on their operating principles. The software listed above will help us illustrate how it works.

So. What do a noise reduction tool and image inpainting have in common? Why is a mask easy to verify, but a generation result is not? And what is this model that requires you to upload five thousand of your frames before it starts being useful? All answers below.

Read more

item.title: Do transformers dream of electric sheep?
item.description:
In 2015, Google released a series of images that looked as if a photograph had been handed over to an artist for editing, and then they forgot to stop him in time. Dozens of eyes appeared in an ordinary landscape, dogs began to be discerned in the clouds, architecture became covered with repeating patterns, and trees turned into something between vegetation and an artist's fantasy. The images quickly spread across the internet, and DeepDream fairly quickly became a distinct visual style.

Initially, the researchers were not so much interested in the images themselves, but in the possibility of understanding what is happening inside the neural network. From the outside, the classifier looks quite simple: a photo enters the model, and at the output a list of probabilities appears — dog, cat, car, airplane. Between these two points lies a huge amount of computation, and from a single model output it is not always clear why it arrived at that particular answer.

You can look at the activation values of individual neurons and channels, build feature maps, and find images that evoke a strong response. There is also a more radical method of investigation: deliberately modifying the input image so that some internal signal of the model becomes stronger. That is how DeepDream came about.

Read more

item.title: What is actually inside ANE, or why ЫЫ cannot be entrusted with reverse engineering
item.description:
The neural network was told: "figure out how it works." After shuffling through gigabytes of matrices, it started digging into the list of classes in AppleNeuralEngine.framework — and found what it was looking for: "40+ private classes, including _ANEInMemoryModel." The code worked. It did what was required — ran the math on the ANE. But there was something… off about it.
